Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images The far right Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US Carmen Aguilar García , Michael Goodier , Pamela Duncan and Dan Sabbagh Sun 9 Aug 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder in Southampton in June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal. Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function. One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK. Seven of the 12 most-read tweets about Belfast and Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America. The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain. Q&A Methodology Show The Guardian collected 43,000 tweets mentioning Belfast, Southampton, Henry Nowak or Vickrum Digwa posted on X during the period of the unrest in both cities. This covered the period from 2 June to the end of 3 June for Southampton and from the evening of 8 June to the end of 9 June for Belfast. For X accounts whose combined tweets reached more than 1,000 views, we extracted their location and the number of times they have changed their username as shown in the “about this account” tab. Using a large language model (LLM), the team first classified which posts were directly related to the protests in Belfast and Southampton, and then categorised them as containing explicit or implicit racist language or anti-immigration comments. For those about Belfast, we also classified tweets as containing calls inciting to violence. A team of three people manually verified more than 5,500 posts, statistically testing the accuracy of the model to be robust and in line with academic standards. Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action. Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content. Their goal, he added, was “to amplify local tragedies and crises, intensify racist narratives, and incite violence in communities they have never set foot in and to whom they have no real connection.” A post from Musk after the life sentencing of the killer of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, who had been falsely accused of racism by police after being stabbed in Southampton, has been viewed more than 28m times. “Legacy mainstream media, same ones who wrote about George Floyd millions of times, are dead silent about Nowak,” Musk posted shortly before 3pm on 2 June, in effect promoting his own platform at a time of heightened tension and disorder in the Hampshire port. View image in fullscreen Elon Musk posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s IPO in June. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Eleven police officers were injured on the night of 2 June in Southampton as people claiming to protest over Nowak’s murder marched to the site of his death. This followed a rally, addressed by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, outside the city’s main police station. Musk is based in the US and has not visited the UK since November 2023. A Guardian analysis last month found he posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s initial public offering in June. Security experts including Fiona Hill, a former adviser to the US and UK governments, have warned that the UK is a soft target for online manipulation by overseas actors because it does not take the idea of civil, or “psychological”, defence seriously. Dr Julia Ebner, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the University of Oxford, said flashpoint episodes such as in Southampton and Belfast had become “strategic events” for far-right actors seeking to amplify and exploit them. “They are using the UK as a negative example, smearing the UK to promote their own narratives of western civilisational decay or social collapse,” Ebner said. “But the other purpose is to influence UK politics, and European politics more widely,” using crisis moments to “promote a strong, strengthened far-right wave across the world”. Four of the top 12 most-seen tweets came from UK accounts: two were by the leader of the Restore Britain party, Rupert Lowe, whom Musk has endorsed; another was from GB News, while the most popular, with 37.6m views, was written by the “anti-woke” rightwing political commentator Konstantin Kisin . Other accounts located in the US were anonymous, though familiar. @EndWokeness posted a blurry still image of a black man attacking a white man in Belfast on 8 June, saying the full video was “too graphic” to post. It attracted 16.3m views. The assault, a stabbing in which the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, lost an eye, prompted three nights of racially motivated rioting targeting non-white people in Belfast. An asylum seeker from Sudan was charged with attempted murder and at least 23 people were arrested. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A vehicle set alight during riots in Belfast in June. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP The @EndWokeness account, which has 3.9m followers, was cited by a parliamentary committee after it amplified a false claim that the 2024 attack in Southport, in which three girls were killed, was carried out by a Muslim man. The account has been linked by an open source analyst to Jack Posobiec, a rightwing influencer who promoted the Pizzagate conspiracy, a false accusation that leading US Democrats were engaged in satanic child abuse at a child-friendly pizza restaurant in Washington DC. Another leading poster was the US rightwing influencer Benny Johnson, who accused the New York Times of writing nothing about Nowak and thousands of pieces about the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 – though Nowak was murdered in the UK. The analysis of the most-viewed accounts did not reveal any posts from Russia or China – both countries that have been behind online disinformation campaigns – though it is possible that posters successfully disguised their locations using virtual private networks (VPNs). X shows location data for most profiles, inferred by the platform from user IP addresses, though government accounts are excluded. Last November, after the feature was introduced, X’s then head of product, Nikita Bier, said it was more than 99% accurate . When it was launched, it revealed that some pro-Scottish-independence accounts were based in Iran. But there were signs of inauthenticity in popular posts. Two of the top most-seen tweets came from the US-based C3 (@C_3C_3) account, accusing “legacy media” of not reporting about the Nowak case. Its profile picture is a baby wearing a Make America Great Again cap; the username has changed 14 times previously. One UK account, which tweeted at least six times about the murder of Nowak, with almost 3,800 combined views, had changed its name more than 400 times. NewsSceneUK – subsequently changed to BritifyFooty – wrote in one tweet about the “huge crowd of patriots outside #Southampton Police Station”. Accounts posting from overseas that changed their usernames more than 20 times included one in Kenya that wrote after the Belfast stabbing: “When the state fails to protect people, the streets find their own language.” Another, from Europe, described the Nowak case as “a globalized, calculated and malicious evil” affecting “every White person and every White nation”. Close to a third – about 13,000 – of the Belfast and Southampton tweets, whether from the UK or abroad, were racist or anti-immigrant, according to the Guardian analysis. When analysed separately, a quarter of the posts that were only about Southampton were racist or anti-immigrant, compared with a third of those that were only about Belfast. One UK-based poster, writing a day after the Belfast stabbing, claimed they hoped the attacker was British-born because “race is the issue, not immigration status”. The post registered 2m views. Valerie Wirtschafter, an expert on online foreign influence operations from the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank, said she believed violent events such as those in Belfast and Southampton were “a point of exploitation” in which “outside agitators” had an opportunity to make a disproportionate impact. Their position was helped by X and other social media companies cutting content moderation, she said, but in particular by “algorithms and how they collide with the basic cognitive processes of humans. We are more attracted to things that are shocking.” Explore more on these topics The far right X Elon Musk Far right Far right (US) Internet Belfast news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/russian-deta.text: World Europe Russian detained in Romania on suspicion of attempted sabotage: Embassy Suspect accused of collecting military information through photos of sensitive facilities Elena Teslova 10 September 2026 • Update : 10 September 2026 Archive MOSCOW The Russian Embassy in Romania said Thursday that it received a notification from the Romanian State Prosecutor's Office about the detention of a Russian citizen. The diplomatic service said the citizen, who is holding a residence permit in Romania, was arrested Tuesday for 30 days on suspicion of "attempting to commit sabotage" on the country's territory. "According to reports that appeared in the Romanian media, citing the Romanian State Security Service and other law enforcement agencies, the Russian is accused of collecting military information through photography and video recording of sensitive facilities in order to organize acts of sabotage and subversion," it said. The embassy emphasized that the published materials consist of "assumptions, speculation, and various kinds of fantasy." "They contain no concrete data confirming the unlawful nature of our citizen's activities or the involvement of Russian state bodies in them. One gets the impression that our compatriot has become the victim of yet another provocation aimed at stirring up anti-Russian sentiment in Romanian society," it said. The embassy said it is closely monitoring the development and is ready to provide the Russian citizen with the necessary consular and legal support. "A request has been sent to the Romanian authorities for a meeting with him," it said. The diplomatic service stressed that the incident "is yet another confirmation that today Russian citizens cannot feel safe, even when they are legally present on the territory of EU countries." "At any moment, they risk becoming victims of unfounded persecution and provocations by Western intelligence services," it said. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story ombudsman_apply_button LATEST NEWS All Yemen sees clashes in Taiz, airstrikes in Saada, Hudaydah amid diplomatic push against Houthis Arab lawmaker criticizes exclusion of Arab lists from Israeli election UN education officials call for urgent action for Gaza children 2 Palestinians killed, 27 injured by Israeli attacks in Gaza Strip Türkiye offers condolences over deaths during military exercise in Kazakhstan New York City mayor slams 'lies' in Netanyahu's UN speech, cites ICC warrant for his arrest France records nearly 7 times more burned land than usual this year See All Canada, Ukraine sign declaration for 100-year partnership Kremlin spokesman says drone posed 'ephemeral threat’ to Zelenskyy's plane

Dariusz Borowicz/Agencja Wyborcza.pl via REUTERS Three people were injured in a stabbing attack at a further education college in Warsaw yesterday, police said, the latest in a series of incidents that have stoked concerns in Poland about copycat violence among young people. On Friday thousands of police visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after two stabbing sprees by teenagers in as many days sparked rumours of potential further attacks, fears that yesterday’s incident is likely to intensify. “At 12.30 today, we received a report of an incident involving the use of a dangerous weapon,” police spokesperson Jakub Filipiak told Reuters. “One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation.” He said the attacker was a 21-year-old student of the college. State news agency PAP reported that the victims were two 17-year-old girls and a 24-year-old woman who had come to submit enrollment documents. Preliminary police findings indicated that the attacker and victims did not know one other, PAP reported. Police said they had inspected some 50,000 facilities since Friday and detained 76 people. Authorities had previously said most of the people detained were teenagers who had made threats online. On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a caretaker and injured two teachers at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital.
